analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers and Medicaid to cover lung cancer screening with no copays or prior-approval hurdles, and expands Medicaid coverage for quitting tobacco.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without action; no vote has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require Medicaid, Medicare, and private health plans to cover annual lung cancer screening for people who meet federal screening guidelines, with no copays and no prior-authorization process, and would ban Medicare Advantage plans and private insurers from requiring prior approval for these scans. It also expands Medicaid so that anyone enrolled — not just pregnant women — can get counseling and medications to quit tobacco, including help quitting vapes and e-cigarettes. It directs the government to run an outreach campaign about who should be screened and to study which groups (like firefighters, veterans, and women under 50) are getting lung cancer but are missed by current screening rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Smokers and former smokers who meet federal screening guidelines — disproportionately lower-income and older Americans — would get lung cancer scans covered with no cost sharing and no prior-approval delays, catching cancers earlier when they are treatable. Medicaid enrollees who want to quit tobacco gain coverage for counseling and cessation medication, including for e-cigarette use. Hospitals and screening clinics gain a steady stream of covered screenings, and tobacco-cessation providers gain a larger market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Smokers and former smokers at high risk

how_it_helps.text: Medicaid must cover annual lung cancer screening for people recommended for it under USPSTF guidelines, with no copays or deductibles, including for people enrolled in Medicaid managed care plans.

Medicare and employer or individual private plans are barred from requiring prior authorization for recommended annual lung cancer screenings, so patients cannot be made to wait for insurer approval first.
Medicaid coverage of counseling and medication to quit tobacco — including vapes and e-cigarettes — expands from pregnant women only to all Medicaid enrollees, with no prior authorization.

HHS would run an education and outreach campaign (authorized at $10 million per year for fiscal 2028–2032) targeted at high-risk individuals, and the GAO would study which groups — such as firefighters, veterans, and women under 50 — are diagnosed with lung cancer but fall outside current screening guidelines.

analysis.who_pays: Federal and state governments pay for the added Medicaid screenings and cessation coverage; private insurers and employers bear the cost of mandated no-cost screening coverage; the federal government also funds the outreach campaign. Insurers and state Medicaid programs lose discretion to require prior authorization on these services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and state Medicaid programs

drawbacks.text: The bill requires coverage without cost sharing or prior authorization across Medicaid, Medicare, and private plans, and insurers and state Medicaid programs bear new mandates without dedicated financing beyond a $50 million outreach authorization — a cost that could show up in premiums or state budgets.

Screening eligibility is frozen to the March 9, 2021 guidelines; if clinical evidence later supports expanding or adjusting screening for other groups, the mandate as written does not automatically follow newer recommendations, and the bill only commissions a study on gaps affecting groups like firefighters, veterans, and women under 50 rather than covering them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are clear and targeted: earlier lung cancer detection saves lives, and removing prior-authorization hurdles and cost sharing removes real barriers that disproportionately affect low-income and Medicaid enrollees. The main cost is money: the federal government and states would pay for more screenings and broader Medicaid cessation coverage, and employers and insurers would absorb a new coverage mandate with no offsetting savings identified in the bill. The outreach program is modestly funded. Overall the benefits appear to outweigh the costs, though the bill leaves open who bears the added insurance costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and has had no further action, so it has not come to a vote.

narrative.text: Durbin introduced the bill on May 19, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
It drew only one cosponsor, a Democrat, giving it a small base of support.
The Finance Committee has taken no action on the bill since referral; it has not been voted out of committee or scheduled for floor debate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: If the outcome holds, insurers and state Medicaid programs avoid the new screening and cessation coverage mandates, and no one yet gains the health benefits the bill would provide.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its screening, cessation-coverage, and outreach provisions.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action on it since May 19, 2026, leaving it without a markup, a committee vote, or a path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Both named sponsors are Democrats and there are no Republican cosponsors, but no floor vote or committee action has occurred, so the partisan split is unknown.

industries.industry: Medicaid managed care organizations and private health insurers
industries.note: Insurers lose the ability to require prior authorization or charge cost sharing for lung cancer screening, a new coverage mandate, but earlier detection and expanded smoking-cessation coverage mostly mean paying for low-cost preventive services rather than big new liabilities.

industries.industry: Hospitals, radiology providers, and lung-screening clinics
industries.note: A guaranteed screening pipeline without prior-authorization friction means more billed screenings, and the bill funds a $10-million-a-year federal outreach campaign that directs people to get screened.
Expanding Medicaid cessation coverage to all enrollees (including e-cigarette cessation) creates a larger market for counseling services and cessation medications, with no prior authorization.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since referral with a single cosponsor and no committee action. Bills in this position rarely reach the floor before a Congress ends unless a chair prioritizes them or they attach to a larger health package, so the most likely path is that it never gets a vote in this Congress.
